One who leaves a jug in the public domain, one carrying a jug who stumbles and breaks it, and one who pours water into the public domain and causes damage. It contains five seifim.
If one leaves a jug in the public domain and another person stumbles over it and breaks it, the passerby is exempt, because people do not ordinarily inspect the road closely while walking. If the passerby is injured by the jug, the jug's owner is liable. This applies even if he renounced ownership of it, because one who abandons a hazard that he had no right to create remains liable.

If it was dark, or he filled the entire road with barrels, he is exempt, etc. This is the Rambam's language in chapter 13 of Hilchot Nizkei Mamon. It appears that even when the road was filled with barrels, the case still assumes that it was possible to go around them, walk along the side, or step carefully over them. Therefore the Mechaber says only that if he stumbled and broke a barrel he is exempt. But where the road was filled so completely that passage was impossible, the Mechaber immediately writes that even if he deliberately breaks the barrels in order to pass, he is exempt. This is also the implication of the Gemara at the beginning of HaManiach, Rashi and Tosafot there, and see the end of siman 379.

mechaber.en: If one pours water into the public domain and another person's utensils become soiled, he is exempt because the water is treated as a pit, and a pit does not impose liability for utensils, whether or not the water was abandoned. If a person slips on the water, falls, and is injured, the one who poured it is liable. Certainly, if the water was absorbed into the ground and became mud that caused damage, it is an actual pit. Liability applies even during the rainy season, when people are permitted to open drains that discharge into the public domain, because permission to discharge does not exempt one from paying for damage. All the more so in summer, when the discharge itself is unauthorized.

א) ברייתא שם פי' רש"י צינור המקלח מי שופכין של תשמיש הבית לר"ה:
beer_hagolah.en:
kuf) Ibid., seif 8, and in the Rambam there, law 12. The Maggid Mishneh writes that this follows Shmuel in the Gemara and not Rav, because all these forms of damage are derivatives of pit, and we do not find liability for utensils damaged by a pit.
reish) Following Shmuel on 28b, whose view we follow.
shin) This too follows Shmuel, who says that the pit for which the Torah imposed liability is liable for its air, and all the more so for the force of impact, 50b, unlike Rav's interpretation on 50a.
tav) In such a case even Rav imposes liability, as explained in the sugya there.
a) The baraita there. Rashi explains that the pipe carries household wastewater into the public domain.

beur_hagra.he: השופך כו'. עבה"ג וכמש"ש ותרתי ל"ל כו':
beur_hagra.en: Your partner is like. And he said to him, “And I shall give him a blessing.”

meirat_einayim.he:
ונפל לארץ והוזק בפר שם כתבתי ל' התוס' דמוקי לה בנפל לארץ שבו המים נשפכו דה"ל כקרקעית הבור דא"כ קשה מ"ש מנתקל בבור ונפל אחורי הבור דפטור כמ"ש בסי' ת"י ע"ש:
נבלעו המים בארץ. ונמחה מהן הארץ עד שנעשה רפש וטיט:
והזיקו דהשתא כו' דוקא הזיקו הא אם מת מזה השור פטור כיון דאין כאן הבל וגם ליתא כאן חבטה דעומק עשרה טפחים וכמ"ש בסי' ת"י בטור ובדברי המחבר דחבטה גובה י' טפחים דוקא בעינן לתשלומי מית' ע"ש:
meirat_einayim.en:
It fell to the ground and was injured. In Derishah I cited Tosafos, who establish the case as one where it fell on the ground onto which the water had spilled, so that the ground is treated like the bottom of the pit. Otherwise it would be difficult to distinguish this from one who trips in a pit and falls outside the pit, where the owner is exempt, as explained in siman 410.
The water was absorbed into the ground. Meaning, the ground was softened by the water until it became mud and mire.
And it caused injury, for now, etc. Specifically injury. If an ox died from this, the owner is exempt, because there is no harmful air and there is not an impact from a depth of ten handbreadths. As explained in siman 410, a ten-handbreadth fall is required for liability for death.
